scenes.heading: Electron configuration
scenes.sub: Why does sodium explode in water while neon does nothing?
scenes.say: Why does sodium explode in water, while neon does nothing at all? The answer is how the electrons are arranged.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Bus passengers fill the front seats first
scenes.science: Electrons fill the lowest-energy shell first
scenes.breaks: Passengers choose seats; electrons just settle into the most stable, lowest-energy arrangement.
scenes.say: Picture a bus where people take the seats nearest the door first: two in the front row, then eight, then eight. Electrons fill the lowest-energy shell, closest to the nucleus, first, and only move out when it's full.
scenes.caption: Picture a bus where people take the seats nearest the door first: 2 in the front row, then 8, then 8. Electrons fill the lowest-energy shell, closest to the nucleus, first, and only move out when it's full.

scenes.heading: Writing a configuration
scenes.say: Find the atomic number. That's how many electrons a neutral atom has. Fill shell one with two, shell two with eight, shell three with eight, then shell four. Then check the numbers add up.
scenes.caption: Find the atomic number. That's how many electrons a neutral atom has. Fill shell 1 with 2, shell 2 with 8, shell 3 with 8, then shell 4. Then check the numbers add up.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: Write the electron configuration of sulfur (Z = 16). What are its group and period?
scenes.say: Sulfur has sixteen electrons. Two go in shell one, eight in shell two, and the last six in shell three. So it's two, eight, six. Three shells means period three. Six valence electrons means group sixteen, because for groups thirteen to eighteen you add ten.
scenes.caption: Sulfur has 16 electrons. 2 go in shell 1, 8 in shell 2, and the last 6 in shell 3: 2, 8, 6. Three shells means period 3. Six valence electrons means group 16, because for groups 13 to 18 you add 10.

scenes.heading: Rows = rings, columns = count
points: Valence electrons: in the outermost shell
scenes.say: Valence electrons are in the outermost shell, and they're the ones that react, like players on the edge of a footy pack. Rows equal rings: the period number is the number of shells. Columns equal count: the group tells you the valence electrons. Same group, same valence electrons, similar properties.

scenes.heading: Lose or gain?
scenes.say: Noble gases have full outer shells, so they hardly react. Other atoms react to get one too. Metals lose their one to three valence electrons: sodium becomes two, eight. Non-metals with five to seven gain or share: chlorine becomes two, eight, eight.
scenes.caption: Noble gases have full outer shells, so they hardly react. Other atoms react to get one too. Metals lose their 1–3 valence electrons: Na⁺ is 2, 8. Non-metals with 5–7 gain or share: Cl⁻ is 2, 8, 8.

scenes.heading: Watch out!
points: Ions lose electrons from the OUTER shell
scenes.say: Watch out! Shell one holds only two. Potassium is two, eight, eight, one, not two, eight, nine. Peel ions like an onion, from the outside, so magnesium becomes two, eight. And helium is the odd one out: two electrons, but in group eighteen, because its only shell is full.
scenes.caption: Watch out! Shell 1 holds only 2. Potassium is 2, 8, 8, 1, not 2, 8, 9. Peel ions like an onion, from the outside, so Mg²⁺ is 2, 8. And helium is the odd one out: 2 electrons, but in group 18, because its only shell is full.

points: Metals lose, non-metals gain or share
scenes.say: Quick recap. For the first twenty elements, shells hold two, eight, eight, two. Period equals shells, group tells you valence electrons. Metals lose electrons, non-metals gain or share, to reach a full outer shell. Now try the practice questions!
scenes.caption: Quick recap. For the first 20 elements, shells hold 2, 8, 8, 2. Period = shells, group tells you valence electrons. Metals lose electrons, non-metals gain or share, to reach a full outer shell. Now try the practice questions!
